sets.approach: Mercury night-side approach. Deep-navy starfield; a huge dark Mercury disc filling the lower right with a thin glowing sunlit rim on its far edge, craters faintly outlined on the dark side; the small BepiColombo stack (gold-foil body, two dark wings, silver cone sunshield) drifts in from the left; setp.t 0..1 = the stack slides toward the planet and the camera pushes; setp.fire 0|1 = four small orange thruster flames ignite under the stack with a soft bloom; setp.glow 'gold'|'red' tints the rim.
sets.stackview: Close view of the stack in space. Deep-navy bg; a big detailed cutaway of the stack: gold-foil MPO body, a grey antenna dish, two long dark solar wings, a silver cone-shaped sunshield hiding the smaller Mio orbiter under it; setp.t 0..1 = slow rotate and drift; setp.label 0|1 = chips MPO and MIO point at the parts; setp.fire 0|1 = four thruster flames burn at the bottom.
sets.route: Inner solar system route map. Deep-navy bg; a glowing yellow Sun at the centre, thin orbit rings for Mercury, Venus and Earth, and a gold dotted spiral path winding inward from Earth; setp.t 0..1 = the path draws on from Earth to Mercury and a tiny probe dot travels along it; setp.marks 0..9 = small numbered flyby dots light up along the path (1 Earth, 2-3 Venus, 4-9 Mercury); setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.sunfall: Falling toward the Sun. Deep-navy bg; a giant glowing orange Sun on the right with big soft rays; a tiny probe on the left with a streaking gold speed trail; setp.t 0..1 = the probe falls toward the Sun and the trail stretches longer; setp.brake 0|1 = orange brake flames burn on the probe's front and the trail shrinks; setp.speed 0..1 = a cyan speedometer arc fills.
sets.energy: Energy comparison. Deep-navy bg; two tall outlined fuel-tank columns side by side: a short one labelled with a tiny Pluto dot and a taller one labelled with a tiny Mercury dot, fluid fills gold; setp.pluto 0..1 = the left tank fills; setp.merc 0..1 = the right tank fills beyond the left; setp.glow 'gold'|'red'.
sets.mercury: Mercury globe close-up. Deep-navy bg; a big grey cratered Mercury sphere with a hard dark/light terminator line, 4 px outline, warm rim light on the sunward side; setp.t 0..1 = the planet turns slowly and the terminator creeps across; setp.core 0|1 = a cutaway shows a huge glowing orange core inside (far bigger than expected); setp.sun 0..1 = a giant orange sun glow grows behind it.
sets.compare: Size comparison of three worlds on a plain deep-navy stage: Moon (small pale grey ball), Mercury (grey ball 1.5x as wide as the Moon, darker), Earth (blue-green ball much bigger); setp.t 0..1 = they slide into line and thin cream width lines draw; setp.mass 0|1 = little scales appear showing Mercury heavier than the Moon (four times).
sets.thermo: Day and night extremes split screen. Left half: blazing white-hot ground under a big sun, heat shimmer; right half: black icy ground with stars and frost; a vertical divider line; setp.t 0..1 = the divider sweeps slowly and the shimmer or frost grows; setp.hot 0..1 = the left half glows orange then white; setp.cold 0..1 = the right half frosts blue.
sets.spin: Mercury day length. Deep-navy bg; a small Mercury ball with a gold marker dot on its surface and a tiny sun far left; a big cream clock-face ring around the ball filled in segments of 58 days; setp.t 0..1 = the ball turns once slowly and the segments fill; setp.day 0..1 = the sunlit half brightens then the night half darkens.
sets.crater: Permanently shadowed polar crater. Deep-navy bg; a deep bowl-shaped crater with a bright sunlit rim at the top and pitch-black floor, pale blue ice crystals glinting on the floor, 4 px outlines; setp.t 0..1 = a thin sunbeam creeps along the rim but never reaches the floor; setp.ice 0..1 = the ice crystals glow cyan.
sets.fault: Spacecraft power fault. Deep-navy bg; the transfer module (a big boxy gold body with two huge dark solar wings and four round ion-thruster nozzles); setp.t 0..1 = slow drift; setp.spark 0..1 = a jagged amber electric spark crackles between the solar wing and a small box on the body, and the nozzle glow dims; setp.dim 0|1 = the nozzle glow dims to a faint ember.
sets.delay: Signal delay diagram. Deep-navy bg; a small blue Earth on the left with a dish, a tiny probe on the right, a long thin cyan line between them with a bright pulse; setp.t 0..1 = the pulse travels from Earth to the probe; setp.back 0..1 = a gold pulse returns; setp.clock 0|1 = a stopwatch face between them shows the elapsed minutes.
sets.timeline: A horizontal mission timeline. Deep-navy bg; a long gold line with milestone dots and cream calendar tags; setp.t 0..1 = the camera pans along the line; setp.now 0..1 = a bright cyan marker glides along and pulses on each dot; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.orbits: Two orbits around Mercury seen from above the pole. Deep-navy bg; a small grey Mercury in the middle, a small tight cyan ellipse (MPO) and a big wide gold ellipse (Mio) both outlined; setp.mpo 0..1 = the cyan ellipse draws on with a dot circling; setp.mio 0..1 = the gold ellipse draws on with a dot circling; setp.split 0|1 = a stacked dot separates into the two dots; setp.t 0..1 = slow camera pull out.
sets.xray: X-ray detector view. Deep-navy bg; a big circular detector screen, 4 px outline, showing a glowing violet-white blob (the Crab Nebula) made of grainy dots; setp.t 0..1 = the grainy dots accumulate and the blob sharpens; setp.slew 0..1 = the screen frame jerks to a new pointing; setp.count 0..55 = a small tick counter of slews.
sets.lab: A bright mission control room. far: wall of dark screens with soft cream charts and a world map; mid: a desk with two laptops, a coffee mug and a sticky note; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim; setp.alert 0..1 = a screen flashes amber with a warning triangle; setp.ok 1 = screens turn green.
sets.dawn: Dawn sky looking east. Deep-navy to peach gradient sky above a dark hill horizon with a few small houses silhouetted; a small bright dot (Mercury) low near the horizon and a much brighter dot (Venus) higher up and to the right, faint stars; setp.t 0..1 = the sky slowly brightens; setp.mark 0..1 = a cyan ring and a label point to Mercury; setp.venus 0|1 = Venus glows.
sets.crash: End of mission. Deep-navy bg; a grey cratered Mercury surface horizon at the bottom with a bright sun-lit edge; a small probe with a long gold trail descends slowly from the top toward it; setp.t 0..1 = the probe descends and the trail lengthens; setp.fuel 0..1 = a small fuel gauge in the corner drains to empty and blinks red.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.
sets.instruments: A bright wall of instruments. Deep-navy bg; a row of eleven small outlined icon tiles (camera, laser, magnet, thermometer, X-ray, dust, spectrometer) arranged on a dark panel, each lighting cream or gold one by one; setp.t 0..1 = the tiles light up in order; setp.laser 0..1 = a thin red laser line sweeps down across a grey globe beside the panel; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.magfield: Magnetic field and exosphere. Deep-navy bg; a grey Mercury with looping violet magnetic field lines around it, a stream of tiny yellow solar-wind dots hitting the field from the left, and a thin pale-yellow haze of sodium atoms trailing away on the right; setp.t 0..1 = the solar wind flows and the lines bend; setp.sodium 0..1 = the haze grows; setp.glow 'violet'|'gold'.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.probe: Icon of the BepiColombo stack: a small gold-foil box body with two dark solar-panel wings, a round grey antenna dish and a silver conical sunshield on top, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds an orange thruster flame at the bottom.
props.thermo: Tall outlined thermometer, cream glass tube, red or blue fluid to pp.frac (0..1), pp.label text beneath in FONTS.ui; pp.color red|cyan.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: Eight years. Ten billion kilometres. Now four thrusters fire.
Miss this burn, and Mercury just flies past.
ESA's plan: capture into orbit on twenty-first November.
So what if you rode that spacecraft?
Welcome to Ifmosphere. Here are the rules.
You ride a stack: a European orbiter with a Japanese one tucked inside.
At launch the whole stack weighed four thousand one hundred kilograms.
film.dir: matter of fact; stress 'four thousand one hundred'

film.vo: Fourteen hundred of those kilograms were just fuel.
Rule one. You can't steer live.
Earth is almost one hundred and fifty million kilometres away.
film.dir: measured; stress 'one hundred and fifty million'

film.vo: Every command takes eight point three minutes to arrive.
Confirmation takes the same again. That's sixteen minutes of silence.
Rule two. It's a one way trip.
And here's the catch. Mercury is a terrible place to arrive.
Think a small planet near the Sun sounds easy? It's the opposite.
Fall toward the Sun, and the Sun speeds you up.
Faster, and faster, and faster.
To get captured, you have to throw that speed away.
ESA says it takes more energy than flying to Pluto.
Pluto. The planet-sized snowball at the edge of everything.
film.dir: wry, a half-beat of disbelief; stress 'edge'

film.vo: So the stack doesn't brake once. It cheats, nine times.
Flyby one is Earth, in April twenty twenty.
Then Venus. Twice. October twenty twenty, and August twenty twenty-one.
Then Mercury itself. Six flybys, each one a gravity brake.
Nine slingshots. A grand total of nine point nine billion kilometres.
That's about sixty-six times the distance from Earth to the Sun.
Remember the rule. No steering live.
Which means the brake burn is a script you wrote years ago.
But first, meet the planet you're aiming at.
Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system.
But it's still half as big again as the Moon.
And four times heavier. That is a lot of planet for its size.
The reason hides inside. An unusually huge metal core.
Why so dense? That's one of the questions BepiColombo came to answer.
Now the neighbourhood. Mercury sits thirty-six million miles from the Sun.
That is just over a third of Earth's distance.
One Mercury day lasts fifty-eight Earth days of spinning.
The sun stays up three months. Then it stays down three months.
film.dir: playful, stretching the words; stress 'three months'

film.vo: In the day the ground reaches four hundred and fifty degrees.
film.dir: hot, heavy; stress 'four hundred and fifty'

film.vo: At night it drops to minus one hundred and eighty.
film.dir: icy, hushed; stress 'minus one hundred and eighty'

film.vo: Hot enough to melt lead, cold enough to freeze air. Same rock.
Yet in the dark craters at the poles, there's ice.
Permanently shadowed. The sunlight never reaches the floor.
So that's your target. Now, what almost went wrong.
Your arrival was meant to be the fifth of December, twenty twenty-five.
Then, in April twenty twenty-four, a power fault.
Unexpected electrical currents, between a solar wing and a power unit.
The ion thrusters lost power. Your engines, running on a diet.
Mission control had one choice. Redo the entire route.
Arrival slipped by almost a whole year, to November twenty twenty-six.
On fifteenth June twenty twenty-six, the ion drive switched off for good.
On third September, the transfer module let go.
About two hundred million kilometres from Earth.
That module had no antenna, no computer. Just a drifting box.

text.text: AN INERT BOX IN SOLAR ORBIT

film.vo: From here on, only the orbiter's chemical thrusters steer you.
So. The burn.
film.dir: a held breath; one beat, then drop

film.vo: You come in over the south pole, on the night side.
Below you, nothing but black rock and a thin line of dawn.
Four of your thrusters fire together.
They push against your speed, every second, for a long burn.
Too short, and you skim away. Too long, and you dive in.
And you cannot touch the controls. Remember the sixteen minutes.
All you can do is watch the dot on the screen.
Then your speed slips below the planet's grip.
Mercury's gravity catches you. You're in orbit.
A wide, lopsided loop: five ninety by eleven thousand six hundred forty kilometres.
Low point, five ninety. High point, so far you almost leave.
Mission control only learns it worked sixteen minutes later.
And remember, this is only one step of many.
ESA calls it a six-month arrival sequence.
Capture is the middle. The best parts come next.
On the ninth and tenth of December, the stack comes apart.
The European orbiter, MPO, lets go of the Japanese one, Mio.
On sixteenth December, Mio's sunshield drops away.
Then the two of you go your separate ways.
MPO drops low: four hundred and eighty by fifteen hundred kilometres.
It circles Mercury every two point three hours.
Mio swings wide: five ninety by eleven thousand six hundred forty.
One lap takes nine point three hours. Long enough for a whole movie.
MPO keeps burning, to settle into its final orbit by March.
Science starts in April twenty twenty-seven.
Two spacecraft at one planet. That has never happened at Mercury.
Before you, only one spacecraft ever orbited Mercury. NASA's MESSENGER.
That makes you second ever. Count Mariner Ten, and you're the third visit.
film.dir: wry, counting on fingers; stress 'second ever'

film.vo: So what does all that work buy you?
MPO carries eleven instruments. Mio carries five.
A laser will map the shape of the entire planet.
Cameras across many colours will read the surface rock.
And an X-ray eye will taste what the ground is made of.
It already passed its first test. Staring at the Crab Nebula.
Thirty-nine hours of looking, in September.
Fifty-five times the spacecraft turned, to nudge the view.
The picture came out slightly sharper than the lab test in twenty fifteen.
Eighty percent of that instrument's technology was brand new.
After eight years in space, its detector shows no radiation damage.
Mio will watch the magnetic field, and the solar wind hitting it.
It will taste the thin sodium haze that trails behind the planet.
Two spacecraft at once means one watches the wind arrive.
While the other measures what it does up close.
One orbiter alone could never do that. Remember the ice?
Scientists hope those spacecraft can finally say what the ice is.
Here's the part nobody warns you about. You're not coming home.
The spacecraft are expected to orbit for about three years.
Then the fuel runs out, they lose height, and they land hard.
Their lead scientist put it simply. Sadly, they are not coming back.
It's a one point six billion euro goodbye, and it's worth every cent.
And you can wave at Mercury yourself, on a clear morning.
On twenty-first November it sits nineteen point six degrees from the Sun.
That's as far from the Sun as it ever gets this time round.
Brighter than almost every star. Find it low in the east.
Remember the cold open. Four thrusters. One burn. Ten billion kilometres.
Now you know why every second of it was a gamble.
Which planet would you try to orbit first?
Tomorrow: another What If.
Eight years to arrive. One planet to learn.

short.vo: You get one burn to catch a planet. Miss it, you fly past.
short.dir: tense then hard stop; stress 'one burn'

short.vo: BepiColombo. Eight years to get here.
Ten billion kilometres, for one tiny window.
Commands take eight minutes. No live steering.
Falling sunward makes you faster. So it has to brake.
Orbiting Mercury costs more energy than reaching Pluto.
So: nine slingshots. Earth, Venus, Mercury.
Then in twenty twenty-four, a power fault weakened its thrusters.
A year late, but still flying.
Today, four thrusters are set to fire over the night side.
If it works, Mercury catches it in a wide, lopsided orbit.
In December, it splits in two.
A Mercury day: three months light, three months dark.
Four hundred fifty degrees. Then minus one eighty.
Yet there's ice in the dark craters.
In about three years, it crashes. No return.
Look east before sunrise. That dot is Mercury.
Full film on the channel. Because out here, you get one burn.
short.dir: friendly, leading back into the start; stress 'one burn'
